event.input: Write a numbered plan with 60 concise one-sentence steps for building a small task tracking application.
Reduce the plan to exactly five concise steps.

event.text:
1. Define the application’s purpose and target users.
2. Identify core workflows for creating, viewing, updating, and deleting tasks.
3. Limit the initial release to essential task tracking features.
4. Write acceptance criteria for each core workflow.
5. Choose a frontend framework suited to the project.
6. Choose a backend framework or managed backend service.
7. Select a database for persistent task storage.
8. Sketch a simple architecture connecting the interface, API, and database.
9. Create a source code repository.
10. Configure formatting, linting, and basic project scripts.
11. Set up local environment variables and exclude secrets from version control.
12. Create separate development and production configurations.
13. Sketch the main task list screen.
14. Sketch the task creation and editing interface.
15. Define responsive layouts for mobile and desktop screens.
16. Choose accessible colors, typography, and control styles.
17. Define task fields, including title, description, status, priority, and due date.
18. Decide whether the application needs user accounts or a single-user model.
19. Define ownership rules if multiple users will store tasks.
20. Create the database schema with appropriate constraints.
21. Add database migrations for repeatable schema changes.
22. Add indexes for commonly filtered and sorted fields.
23. Seed development data with representative tasks.
24. Define API routes and consistent response formats.
25. Implement database access through a dedicated data layer.
26. Implement task creation with server-side validation.
27. Implement task retrieval with pagination.
28. Implement retrieval of an individual task.
29. Implement updates to editable task fields.
30. Implement task deletion with appropriate safeguards.
31. Add authentication if user accounts are required.
32. Enforce task ownership on every protected API operation.
33. Configure HTTPS, allowed origins, and request size limits.
34. Add consistent API error handling without exposing sensitive details.
35. Build the application shell and navigation.
36. Build the task list with clear status and priority indicators.
37. Add loading, empty, and error states to the task list.
38. Build the task creation form.
39. Add client-side validation and accessible field error messages.
40. Connect task creation to the API.
41. Build the task editing interface.
42. Connect task updates to the API.
43. Add a quick action for marking tasks complete.
44. Add task deletion with confirmation or an undo option.
45. Add filters for task status and priority.
46. Add sorting by due date and creation time.
47. Add a simple task title search.
48. Keep interface state synchronized after successful API operations.
49. Handle failed requests with clear messages and retry options.
50. Verify keyboard navigation, focus behavior, and screen reader labels.
51. Write unit tests for validation and task business rules.
52. Write API integration tests for successful and invalid requests.
53. Test authentication and ownership boundaries when accounts are enabled.
54. Write end-to-end tests for the core task workflows.
55. Test responsive layouts across common browsers and screen sizes.
56. Fix defects and check performance with a realistic task dataset.
57. Configure automated checks and a production deployment pipeline.
58. Deploy the application and run production smoke tests.
59. Set up error monitoring, database backups, and recovery instructions.
60. Collect user feedback and prioritize improvements for the next release.

2. Choose the technology stack and set up the project and database.
3. Build validated task APIs with authentication and ownership checks if needed.
4. Create a responsive interface for managing, filtering, sorting, and searching tasks.
5. Test functionality, accessibility, and security, then deploy, monitor, and gather feedback.
